chunks: Component-by-component loss and ripple. The question: Component-by-component analysis on efficiency and ripple impact.
A buck converter wastes a little power as heat in almost every part. Each part also shapes the ripple on the output.
Going part by part shows where the heat comes from and which part controls which ripple. This is how you find what to fix.
Think of a water delivery system with a pump, valves, long pipes and a storage tank. Every valve and pipe leaks or resists a little, so some energy is lost at each stage.
The tank decides how steady the final flow is. You can ask of each piece two questions: how much does it waste, and how does it affect the smoothness?
The analogy is loose on one point: in a buck, a part wastes power in two different ways (while on, and while changing state).
Loss budget of the reference converter by component.
The two FETs and the inductor account for 97% of the loss; the capacitors are nearly invisible on the efficiency side, though they decide the ripple.
Blue is conduction, orange switching-related, purple gate-drive/fixed, green core loss.
Conduction loss: power lost as heat because current passes through a resistance, I to the 2R .
Switching loss: energy lost each time a switch turns on or off, so it grows with frequency. DCR: the DC resistance of the inductor winding.
ESR: the small resistance inside a capacitor. Efficiency: output power divided by input power ("Why buck beats LDO efficiency").
A 12 volts to 3. 3 volts buck delivers 2 amps, so the output power is 3. 3 times 2 equals 6. 6 watts. Suppose the parts add up to 0.
46 watts of loss: the switches (FETs) and the inductor take most of it. The input power is 6. 6 + 0. 46 = 7. 06 watts, so efficiency is 6. 6 over 7. 06 about 93. 5 % .
The output ripple, meanwhile, comes from the inductor and output capacitor, not from the FETs. That is the whole idea.

The high-side FET has conduction loss D I to the 2R and the largest switching loss; the low-side FET has the largest conduction loss plus dead-time and recovery loss; the driver adds Q gVf and quiescent current; the inductor loses in DCR and core and sets the ripple current; the output capacitor barely affects efficiency but sets the voltage ripple through C and ESR; the input capacitor carries pulsed current and sets input ripple and spikes.
In a 12 volts to 3. 3 volts, 2 amps example, about 460 milliwatts total: low-side about 180, high-side about 140, inductor about 120."
